summary: Describes extensions to the LISP data plane header that support multiprotocol encapsulation and allow new protocol capabilities to be introduced. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: The LISP envelope had room for only one kind of letter. This adds a label that says what is inside, so many kinds can be carried.

subtitle: A small change to the LISP header that says what is inside the packet, so LISP can carry Ethernet, NSH and more.

tldr.problem: The LISP data plane header had no field naming the payload, so LISP could only carry IPv4 or IPv6 packets, while similar encapsulations such as VXLAN could carry Ethernet.
tldr.mechanism: A previously reserved flag, the P-bit, signals that an 8-bit Next Protocol field is present, naming the payload (IPv4, IPv6, Ethernet, NSH or a shim header).
tldr.outcome: LISP can carry multiple protocols and be extended with new data plane functions. When the P-bit is used, Echo-Noncing and Map-Versioning are no longer available in the header.

today: RFC 9305 is a Proposed Standard from October 2022. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why LISP Needs a Next Protocol Field
sections.content:
The LISP data plane, defined in RFC 9300, wraps IPv4 or IPv6 packets in a LISP header and outer UDP/IP transport. The header does not say what it encloses, so it can only carry IP. Other encapsulations, most notably VXLAN (RFC 7348), use a similar header to carry Layer 2 protocols such as Ethernet.

This document extends the LISP header to indicate the inner protocol, enabling Ethernet, IP or any other protocol while staying compatible with existing LISP deployments. Since all reserved header bits have been allocated, it also lets new data plane functions be added through shim headers, for example Group-Based Policy or IOAM metadata.
sections.eli5: A mail envelope used to hold only one kind of letter. Now there is a spot on the outside to write what kind of letter is inside.

sections.title: The LISP-GPE Header
sections.content:
The LISP header has flag bits, a Nonce/Map-Version field and an Instance ID/Locator-Status-Bits field. Flag bit 5 is the last reserved bit. LISP-GPE makes two changes: it defines that bit as the P-bit, and it defines a Next Protocol field.

If the P-bit is 0, the header is bit-by-bit equivalent to RFC 9300. If it is 1, the lower 8 bits of the first 32-bit word carry the Next Protocol. Bits N, E and V and bits 8 to 23 of the field MUST be set to zero on transmission and MUST be ignored on receipt. Features like Echo-Noncing and Map-Versioning can be recreated with LISP-GPE shim headers.
sections.eli5: One tiny switch on the envelope says there is a label. When it is on, the label says what is inside, and a few old features switch off.

sections.title: Next Protocol Values and Shim Headers
sections.content:
The values defined are 0x01 IPv4, 0x02 IPv6, 0x03 Ethernet and 0x04 Network Service Header (NSH, RFC 8300); 0x00 is reserved. Values 0x7E, 0x7F, 0xFE and 0xFF are for experimentation and testing, and 0x80 to 0xFD are for protocols encoded as generic shim headers.

All shim protocols MUST begin with a 32-bit word: Type, Length (in 4-octet units, not counting the first 4 octets), Reserved, and Next Protocol. When shim headers are used with protocols from 0x00 to 0x7F, all shim headers MUST come first. Shim headers let an xTR keep known headers in the fast path (typically an ASIC) while pushing the rest to the slow path.
sections.eli5: The label has a code for each kind of payload. Some codes are for add-on sticky notes that go on the envelope first.

sections.title: Congestion, Checksums and Header Mapping
sections.content:
LISP-GPE is meant for controlled environments, such as one operator or adjacent cooperating operators, following the UDP guidelines in RFC 8085. It has no congestion control of its own, so it MUST be used with congestion-controlled traffic or inside a traffic-managed network.

The outer UDP checksum SHOULD be used over IPv4. Over IPv6 a UDP checksum MUST be used by default. An operator MAY configure a zero checksum in a traffic-managed controlled environment if corruption is very unlikely, measured to be tolerably low, or the payload tolerates it. Then the ETR SHOULD check the source and destination IPv6 addresses, and measures SHOULD keep such traffic off the general Internet.

For IP payloads, ECN handling MUST follow RFC 6040. For Ethernet, the 802.1Q Priority Code Point MAY be mapped to the DSCP, and the VLAN ID MAY be mapped to the LISP Instance ID.
sections.eli5: The envelope does not slow down traffic by itself, so it should travel on roads the owner manages. The check number on the outside matters more on the harder roads.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
LISP-GPE uses the same UDP destination port as LISP, 4341. An encapsulator MUST NOT send the P-bit format to a router that has not indicated support, because that router would ignore the P-bit and misinterpret other header fields. When encapsulating IP to a non-LISP-GPE router, the P-bit MUST be 0.

How an xTR discovers its peers' capabilities is out of scope. Since the target is a traffic-managed controlled environment, ITR/ETR configuration mechanisms may be used.
sections.eli5: Do not use the new labeled envelope with a mail carrier who has not learned it, or they will read the wrong thing.

sections.title: The Next Protocol Registry
sections.content: IANA created the "LISP-GPE Next Protocol" registry of 8-bit values, holding the assignments above. New values are assigned under the Specification Required policy, and the protocols do not themselves need to be IETF Standards Track.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of label codes, and new codes can be added when someone writes down what they mean.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
LISP-GPE security is similar to what RFC 7835 documents for LISP. As with many encapsulations with optional extensions, an on-path adversary can change the packet, including the P-bit, to alter or remove payload, or to claim any payload type. Integrity protection such as IPsec SHOULD be used by extensions that want protection against on-path attackers.

Spoofing, flooding and traffic redirection may depend on the particular payload protocol.
sections.eli5: Anyone along the road could change the label or the letter. Locking the envelope, as IPsec does, keeps it safe.
